messages.body_plain:
Dear Subhasree,

There is your problem. Your network has 100% reciprocated ties. Thus the
parameter tends to infinity and is therefore impossible to estimate.
It seems that you have an undirected network and thus a mutual parameter is
unnecessary for your model, but you should specify the network as
undirected.

If this level reciprocity is just a "coincidence" and the network is truely
undirected and could have unreciprocated ties, then I think your best
option would berunning a Bayesian ERGM and specify a weakly informative
prior for the reciprocity parameter (e.g mean = 0, SD = 3). By doing so
your model will estimate a strongly positive reciprocity parameter, but
will not run into degeneracy problems.
Of course it would be much easier to just make it undirected, exclude the
mutual paramter and stick to ERGM.

Best Regards,

Robert Krause

messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,
I have a reviewer's comment running through my head lately. I was hoping
you guys can help me understand his concerns and perhaps figure out a
solution.

I am running a dyadic dependent model. I am looking at factors (specific to
the node, edge and network ) that might affect the presence of an edge in
my network. I am using an exponential random model with just the count of
edges as a null model.
One of the reviewers is wondering if some of the network factors that I
found significant in my final model  (indegree and outdegree for example)
might just be an artificial consequence of the presence of hubs (i.e. they
help to improve the fit for nodes of high degree) or if they correspond to
a real effect.  The reviewer is proposing to rerun the model with
significant network variables only as a null model instead of the count of
edges model.

The way I see it ( please, correct me if I am wrong) is that by adding
particular network factors (indegree and outdegree for example) we are
somehow controlling for them in the model similarly to how we address for
confounders in a regular logistic regression model.

I will be happy to give more details if needed.

Thank you all,
Jaber

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jaber,

The choice of null model depends on the substantive theoretical context.

If your context is known to have hubs -- i.e., there's a pre-existing 
explanation for their presence -- then yes, there's no reason to test the 
hypothesis that they exist.  In that case, it would be appropriate to 
include them in the "null" model, to control for their effects when 
testing any additional terms.  I can imagine an example would be internet, 
telephone or airline routing networks, where we know the network has 
been explicitly designed with a hub structure.

If there is no such exogenous process at work, then testing for the 
presence of degree effects would make sense.  An example might be 
friendship networks.

hth,
Martina

Network Modeling for Epidemics (NME) is a 5-day short course at the
University of Washington that provides an introduction to stochastic
network models for infectious disease transmission dynamics, with a focus
on empirically based modeling of HIV transmission. It is a ''hands-on''
course, using the EpiModel software package in R (www.epimodel.org).
EpiModel provides a unified framework for statistically based modeling of
dynamic networks from empirical data, and simulation of epidemic dynamics
on these networks. It has a flexible open-source platform for learning and
building several types of epidemic models: deterministic compartmental,
stochastic individual-based, and stochastic network models. Resources
include simple models that run in a browser window, built-in generic models
that provide basic control over population contact patterns, pathogen
properties and demographics, and templates for user-programmed modules that
allow EpiModel to be extended to the full range of pathogens, hosts, and
disease dynamics for advanced research. This course will touch on the
deterministic and individual-based models, but its primary focus is on the
theory, methods and application of network models.


The course uses mornings for lectures, and afternoons for labs with
students working in small groups. On the final day, students have the
option of developing an EpiModel prototype for their own research projects,
with input from the instructors, which includes the lead EpiModel software
developer, Dr. Samuel Jenness.

Returning students: We encourage previous attendees with active modeling
projects to apply to return for a refresher course. The EpiModel package
has been significantly enhanced over the last few years. Returning students
with active projects will have the opportunity to work with course
instructors to address key challenges in the design of their network model
code.

The course will be taught from Monday, August 20 to Friday, August 24 on
the University of Washington campus in Seattle.

Course fee is $600. Travel and accommodation costs are the responsibility
of the participant, although discounted hotel rates are available. We offer
a limited number of fee waivers for pre-doctoral students or for attendees
from low income countries.  These cover waiver of the registration fee
only; travel and accommodation are still the responsibility of the fee

and a response required by June 1. A waitlist will be established with
rolling admission through June 30.

Apply online at https://catalyst.uw.edu/webq/survey/morrism/347069

I am currently trying to fit a temporal ERGM to a dataset containing information on the sitting of teenagers during their meals in a holidays? summer camp. messages.body_plain:
Hi Timoth?e,

I'll try to offer my perspective on this. I assume you have consulted
the following forthcoming paper, which will appear very soon (in fact, I
have just returned the proofs):

Leifeld, Philip, Skyler J. Cranmer and Bruce A. Desmarais (2018):
Temporal Exponential Random Graph Models with btergm: Estimation and
Bootstrap Confidence Intervals. Journal of Statistical Software 83(6):
1-36. http://dx.doi.org/10.18637/jss.v083.i06

The DOI is not working yet, but you can download a copy here for now:
https://www.philipleifeld.com/cms/upload/v83i06.pdf

About your questions:

1. STERGM takes the changes between t_1 and t_2 and models them using an
ERGM. Since there are two transition matrices -- a matrix with new ties
and a matrix with disappearing ties -- you necessarily have to estimate
two separate models. This can be good if you have separate theories on
tie formation and dissolution and if the two processes do not interact.
A TERGM, in contrast, models t_2 and can include temporal dependencies
that encompass changes from t_1 to t_2 as model terms. So it is fair to
say that changes are accommodated in both model types, but in a
different way: in the dependent variable in the STERGM and in the
independent variables in the TERGM.

This also means that dependencies over more than two consecutive time
points can in principle be included in the TERGM, for example triadic
closure over three time points or autoregressive lags of more than one
time point or temporal trends or breaks, depending on what makes sense
theoretically.

Since the TERGM models network states (even if as a function of changes
and thereby possibly as a temporal process), it would be wrong to say
that it can only model formation but not dissolution since both go into
the state that is being modeled.

You can also say that both the TERGM and the STERGM are essentially
pooled ERGMs over multiple time points, but the STERGM would be more
precisely characterized as a pooled ERGM of the transition matrices
while the TERGM is a pooled ERGM of the list of networks. At least in
its simplest form if you do not include any temporal dependencies like
delayed reciprocity or triadic closure, autoregressive memory terms,
temporal trends etc.

Whether you should use a STERGM or a TERGM depends likely on the
following questions:

a. Are you theoretically interested in explaining the transition
matrices (e.g., the transitions from not sitting together to sitting
together and from sitting together to not sitting together) or in the
network matrices (e.g., sitting together or not sitting together)? In
the former case, use a STERGM; in the latter case, use a TERGM.

b. Do you have theoretical reasons to think that the act of
transitioning from sitting together to not sitting together is
independent of the transitioning from not sitting together to sitting
together, or are they a joint process that should be modeled in the same
equation? In the former case, use a STERGM, in the latter a TERGM.

c. Do you have reason to believe that your data-generating process is a
Markov process in the sense that the network at t_3 is only affected by
the network at t_2 but not by the network at, say, t_1 or t_0, or can
there be longer-term dependencies? In the former case, either model is
fine, in the latter case the TERGM can do this.

d. Do you have many consecutive networks and are these networks large,
such that MCMC-MLE estimation is not feasible, or is MCMC-MLE a feasible
estimation strategy in terms of degeneracy and computation time? If this
is an issue, the btergm procedure is your friend. If not, use mtergm for
MCMC-MLE or use a STERGM.

e. Do you need to model time trends? For example, does your network get
denser or sparser over time (linearly, with a polynomial function of
time, as a step function etc.)? Do you need to interact these time
trends with covariates, for example for modeling differential effects of
covariates before and after some event? If so, the timecov term in the
btergm package can do this.

2. I'm not sure about data requirements in the tergm package, but in the
btergm package you can supply consecutive matrices or networks with
different dimensions as long as the matrices or networks have (node)
labels. The package will automatically take care of composition change.

I don't have a good solution for choosing the optimal duration of the
time window for aggregating your events into time slices, but you could
play with different aggregation rules and check if there is a massive
difference or if the results are relatively robust with regard to the
length of the time window.

The problem you are describing with on-off-on relationships can either
be solved by aggregating into larger time windows or, possibly, by
increasing K in the TERGM. This means you would condition not just on
the previous time point, but possibly on (functions of) the pre-previous
time point or interactions between that and the current or previous time
point. For example, you could add a list of covariate matrices that
specify a temporal lag of the relationships at t over the last three
time points t_-1, t_-2, and t_-3, with a geometric temporal weight, such
as x_ij^t = N_ij^t_-1 + (0.5 * N_ij^t_-2) + (0.25 * N_ij^t_-3) or
something like that. It depends on what you think captures your temporal
dependence best, and you can test this through goodness-of-fit measures.
On top of these temporal specifications, you can then include other
temporal or within-time-step effects, both endogenous and exogenous.

As far as I know, valued-edge ERGMs (e.g., GERGM) and TERGMs have not
been combined so far, but I may be wrong.

Best regards,

Philip

as x_ij^t = N_ij^t_-1 + (0.5 * N_ij^t_-2) + (0.25 * N_ij^t_-3) or
something like that. It depends on what you think captures your temporal
dependence best, and you can test this through goodness-of-fit measures.
On top of these temporal specifications, you can then include other
temporal or within-time-step effects, both endogenous and exogenous.

As far as I know, valued-edge ERGMs (e.g., GERGM) and TERGMs have not
been combined so far, but I may be wrong.

Best regards,

Philip

This may be of interest to some folks here.

The workshop focuses on epidemics, but the methods and software (based on

############################################################################

Network Modeling for Epidemics
Summer short course at the University of Washington
20-24 August, 2018

Network Modeling for Epidemics (NME) is a 5-day short course at the University 
of Washington that provides an introduction to stochastic network models for 
infectious disease transmission dynamics, with a focus on empirically based 
modeling of HIV transmission. It is a ''hands-on'' course, using the EpiModel 
software package in R (www.epimodel.org). EpiModel provides a unified framework 
for statistically based modeling of dynamic networks from empirical data, and 
simulation of epidemic dynamics on these networks. It has a flexible 
open-source platform for learning and building several types of epidemic 
models: deterministic compartmental, stochastic individual-based, and 
stochastic network models. Resources include simple models that run in a 
browser window, built-in generic models that provide basic control over 
population contact patterns, pathogen properties and demographics, and 
templates for user-programmed modules that allow EpiModel to be extended to the 
full range of pathogens, hosts, and disease dynamics for advanced research. 
This course will touch on the deterministic and individual-based models, but 
its primary focus is on the theory, methods and application of network models.

The course uses mornings for lectures, and afternoons for labs with students 
working in small groups. On the final day, students have the option of 
developing an EpiModel prototype for their own research projects, with input 
from the instructors, which includes the lead EpiModel software developer, Dr. 
Samuel Jenness.

Returning students: We encourage previous attendees with active modeling 
projects to apply to return for a refresher course. The EpiModel package has 
been significantly enhanced over the last few years. Returning students with 
active projects will have the opportunity to work with course instructors to 
address key challenges in the design of their network model code.

Dates and location:

The course will be taught from Monday, August 20 to Friday, August 24 on the 
University of Washington campus in Seattle.

Costs:

Course fee is $600. Travel and accommodation costs are the responsibility of 
the participant, although discounted hotel rates are available. We offer a 
limited number of fee waivers for pre-doctoral students or for attendees from 
low income countries.  These cover waiver of the registration fee only; travel 
and accommodation are still the responsibility of the fee waiver recipient.

Application dates and decision dates:

*    Apr 1: Fee-waiver application deadline. Decisions will be made by Apr 15, 
and response required by May 1.

*    May 1:  General application deadline. Decisions will be made by May 15 and 
a response required by June 1. A waitlist will be established with rolling 
admission through June 30.

Application:

Apply online at https://catalyst.uw.edu/webq/survey/morrism/347069

Course website and more information: http://statnet.github.io/nme

Please free to share widely!

Yours,
Martina Morris, Steve Goodreau and Samuel Jenness

Hi Lin -

The good news is that, if it fits sometimes and simulations look good, 
then you know your model is indeed generally estimable, and not 
degenerate. That said, it sounds like your estimation algorithm 
sometimes wanders into degenerate or near-degenerate territory. I'd try 
varying some of the ergm control parameters from their defaults to add 
more stability to the estimation procedure - it'll take longer, but 
hopefully lead more consistently to successful estimation.? Common ones are:

- increasing MCMLE.maxit, MCMC.interval, MCMC.burnin, and/or MCMC.samplesize

- decreasing MCMLE.steplength

And there are many more to explore at ?control.ergm.

If you wish a deep theoretical dive into this concept of stability, one 
place to start is Schweinberger 2011 
(https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3405854/). Not for the 
statistically faint of heart though! :-)

 Edge attribute names not shown

When I estimate an ERG model for such a large network, I run into the
following error:

> modelx <- ergm(netx ~ edges + edgecov(mg) + edgecov(m4) + edgecov(mt))
[1] "Warning:  This network is allowed to contain loops"
Error in ergm.getglobalstats(nw, model, response = response) :
  long vectors (argument 13) are not supported in .C

I believe this error message occurs because R is trying to pass a long
vector via .C, which doesn't support long vectors.

Did anyone else run into similar issues? If so, how did you engage with
this issue?

Any help is much appreciated. Thank you!

Dear Frank,

TL;DR: The edgecov() terms are very memory-inefficient. I don't know what these mg/m4/mt matrices represent, but if they can be generated from, say, nodal information, you can implement a custom ergm term that gets passed nodal information and generates them on the fly.

Technical explanation: Internally, ergm concatenates covariate vectors and passes them on to the C code, where they get unpacked. Each edgecov() term passes an n*n matrix, and in your case, each of these matrices is 270000^2 elements long. Three of them add up to a vector of length 2187000000 which is longer than the greatest integer that can be represented using the basic integer type (2147483647). Now, R can handle vectors like that, but not through the .C() interface.

I hope this helps,
Pavel

messages.body_plain:
Greetings statnet cognoscenti,
     The ergm package has a setting in the as.network() function for whether or not hyper-edges are allowed, but this setting is currently ignored (in version 3.8.0). Is this an area of active development? Is anyone on the mailing list aware of other resources which might be useful for those interested in modeling hypergraphs? I am aware of the hypergraph package (https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/hypergraph.html), but not of any tools at this point that go beyond this.

Best,
-tyler
